abstract: The interval result of Evertse and Ferretti (2013) concerns a tuple $L$ of linear forms and one tuple $c$ of weights. It says that the parameters $Q$ for which the twisted height $H_{L,c,Q}$ has a small value outside an exceptional subspace $T(L,c)$ lie in $O(\delta^{-2}\log\delta^{-1})$ intervals $[Q_i,Q_i^{\omega})$. We prove this for a whole set $\mathcal{C}$ of weights with the same forms. At most $J$ subspaces $T(L,c)$ occur, where $J$ depends only on the dimension and on the number of places, and one family of $O(\delta^{-2}\log\delta^{-1})$ intervals serves every $c\in\mathcal{C}$ at once. Neither count depends on $\mathcal{C}$. In applications of Bugeaud-Evertse type the solutions are sorted into about $\varepsilon^{-1}$ classes with the same forms and different weights, and one application now serves all classes. We deduce three complexity bounds. For a real algebraic irrational number $\xi$, the number $p(n,\xi,b)$ of blocks of length $n$ in its base-$b$ expansion satisfies $\limsup p(n,\xi,b)/(n(\log n)^\eta)=\infty$ for every $\eta<1/2$; Bugeaud and Evertse proved this for $\eta<1/11$. The same holds for the continued fraction expansion of an algebraic number of degree at least three, and for the steering word of $(3/2)^n$. We explain why $1/2$ is the limit of the method. All results are machine-verified in Lean~4.
hook: Algebraic irrational numbers have digit-block complexity beyond n(log n)^eta for eta below 1/2, up from 1/11.
summary: The paper strengthens a known lower bound on how many distinct digit blocks an irrational algebraic number must contain, raising the exponent from 1/11 to 1/2. It does so by extending an interval result of Evertse and Ferretti to many weights at once, and the same bound holds for continued fractions of degree three or higher. The authors say 1/2 is the limit of this method, and the proofs are checked in Lean 4.
title: The Evertse-Ferretti interval result for a set of weights, and the exponent $1/2$ in three complexity bounds
